And, oh, that eightfold fence! |} The child born to Susanoo and Kushinadahime is variously identified as [[Yashimajinumi]] in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and Ōnamuchi ([[Ōkuninushi]]) in the ''Shoki'''s main account.Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj027.htm Section XX.—The August Ancestors of the Deity-Master-of-the-Great-Land.]{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |year=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |page=92}}{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=54}} ====Variants==== [[File:Mt.Sentsuzan.jpg|thumb|290px|{{ill|Mount Sentsū|en|Mount Sentsū|qid=Q6923566|lt=Mount Sentsū|1=Mount Sentsū}} as seen from [[:en:Okuizumo, Shimane|Okuizumo]] with the Hii River in the foreground]] While most accounts identify the headwaters of the river Hi in Izumo (肥河 / 簸之川, ''Hi-no-Kawa'', identified with the {{ill|Hii River|en|Hii River|qid=Q11500714|lt=Hii River|1=Hii River}} in modern {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}) as the place where Susanoo descended, one variant in the ''Shoki'' instead has Susanoo arriving at the upper reaches of the river E (可愛之川 ''E-no-Kawa'') in the province of {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|qid=Q965029|lt=Aki|1=Aki Province}} (identified with the {{ill|Gōnokawa River|en|Gōnokawa River|qid=Q2090210|lt=Gōnokawa River|1=Gōnokawa River}} in modern {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|qid=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}}). In this version, Inadahime - whose name is given here as 'Makamifuru-Kushiinadahime' (真髪触奇稲田媛) - is not yet born when Susanoo slew the Yamata no Orochi.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=55}}{{cite book |last1=Kuroita |first1=Katsumi |title=Kundoku Nihon Shoki, vol. 1 (訓読日本書紀 上巻) |date=1943 |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |pages=69–71 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1904260/37}} {{blockquote|text=In one writing it is said:—"At this time Sosa no wo no Mikoto went down and came to the head-waters of the River Ye, in the province of Aki. There was there a God whose name was Ashi-nadzu-te-nadzu. His wife's name was Inada no Miya-nushi Susa no yatsu-mimi. This Deity was just then pregnant, and the husband and wife sorrowed together. So they informed Sosa no wo no Mikoto, saying:—'Though we have had born to us many children, whenever one is born, an eight-forked serpent comes and devours it, and we have not been able to save one. We are now about to have another, and we fear that it also will be devoured. Therefore do we grieve.' Sosa no wo no Mikoto forthwith instructed them, saying:—'You must take fruit of all kinds, and brew from it eight jars of sake, and I will kill the serpent for you.' The two Gods, in accordance with his instructions, prepared sake. When the time came for the child to be born, the serpent came indeed to the door, and was about to devour the child. But Sosa no wo no Mikoto addressed the serpent, and said:—'Thou art an Awful Deity. Can I dare to neglect to feast thee?' So he took the eight jars of sake, and poured one into each of its mouths. The serpent dRank it up and fell asleep. Sosa no wo no Mikoto drew his sword and slew it. [...]
Afterwards the child who was born of Inada no Miya-nushi Susa no yatsu-mimi, namely Ina-gami (''{{ill|Sic|en|Sic|qid=Q192003|lt=Sic|1=Sic}}'') Furu-kushi-nada-hime, was removed to the upper waters of the river Hi, in the province of ldzumo, and brought up there. After this Sosa no wo no Mikoto made her his consort, and had by her a child, whose descendant in the sixth generation was [[Ōkuninushi|Oho-na-muchi no Mikoto]]."|author=translation by William George Aston}} A legend associated with [[:ja:八重垣神社|Yaegaki Shrine]] in {{ill|Matsue|en|Matsue|qid=Q207321|lt=Matsue|1=Matsue}}, Shimane Prefecture claims that Susanoo hid Kushinadahime in an "eightfold fence" (''yaegaki'') in the forest within the shrine's precincts during his battle with the Yamata no Orochi.{{cite web |title=八重垣神社について |url=https://yaegakijinja.or.jp/origin |website=【公式】八重垣神社 (Yaegaki Shrine Official Website) |access-date=2020-03-30}} ===In the Izumo ''Fudoki''=== [[File:Yaegaki Jinja hekiga.jpg|thumb|160px|left|{{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}} wall painting depicting Kushinadahime ([[Yaegaki Shrine]], {{ill|Matsue|en|Matsue|qid=Q207321|lt=Matsue|1=Matsue}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}})]] A legend recorded in the Izumo ''[[Fudoki]]'' concerning the township of Kumatani (熊谷郷) in {{ill|Iishi District, Shimane|en|Iishi District, Shimane|qid=Q1349339|lt=Iishi District|1=Iishi District, Shimane}} (part of the modern city of [[:en:Unnan, Shimane|Unnan]] in Shimane{{cite web |title=飯石郡の村々 |url=https://www.pref.shimane.lg.jp/life/bunka/bunkazai/izumo_fuudo/mura/iish2.html |website=Shimane Prefectural Government Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19}}) relates that Kushinadahime - as 'Kushiinada-Mitoyomanurahime' - passed through the area while she was about to give birth. The township's name is said to come from her exclamation: "How deep and well hidden (''kumakumashiki'') this valley (''tani'') is!"{{cite book |last1=Kurita |first1=Hiroshi |title=標註古風土記 出雲 (Hyōchū Kofudoki: Izumo) |date=1931 |publisher=Ō-Oyakama Shoten. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dSqbfMx0ErgC}}{{cite book |title=Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries. |date=1997 |publisher=Association for Asian Studies, Inc. |translator=Aoki, Michiko Y.|page=40}} ===In the Hōki ''Fudoki''=== An excerpt claimed to be from the now-lost ''Fudoki'' of {{ill|Hōki Province|en|Hōki Province|qid=Q1053703|lt=Hōki Province|1=Hōki Province}} (modern western {{ill|Tottori Prefecture|en|Tottori Prefecture|qid=Q133935|lt=Tottori Prefecture|1=Tottori Prefecture}}) relates that Inadahime fled to Hōki and hid in the mountains when the Yamata no Orochi was about to devour her. The province's name (originally ''Hahaki'') is here said to be derived from her cry for help: "Mother, come!" (''haha kimase''){{cite book |last1=Yano |first1=Harumichi |title=神典翼 第3巻 (Shinten'yoku, vol. 3) |date=1939 |publisher=Kokumin Seishin Bunka Kenkyūjo |page=130|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tFX2M_MiEeYC&pg=PP142}}{{cite web |title=山陰道の旧国－１（伯耆国・Inaba Province ） |url=http://houki.yonago-kodaisi.com/F-geo-Kyuukoku-B1.html |website=米子（西伯耆）・山陰の古代史 (Yonago (Nishi-Hōki) / San'in no Kodaishi) |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}}{{cite web |title=伯耆 (Hōki) |url=http://www.nihonjiten.com/data/247618.html |website=Nihon Jiten (日本辞典) - Japan Dictionary |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} == Worship == [[File:Front shrine of the Hikawa shrine.jpg|thumb|[[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]] in [[:en:Saitama, Saitama|Saitama]], {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture|1=Saitama Prefecture}}]] As with other Shinto ''kami'', Kushinadahime is venerated at many shrines across Japan, usually together with her husband Susanoo but also sometimes by herself or with other (related or unrelated) deities. Some examples of Shinto shrines which enshrine her are as follows. * [[:ja:稲田神社 (奥出雲町)|Inada Shrine]] in [[:en:Okuizumo, Shimane|Okuizumo]], {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}{{cite web |title=稲田神社 |url=https://okuizumo.org/jp/guide/detail/215/ |website=奥出雲町公式観光ガイド (The Official Okuizumo Travel Guide) |access-date=2020-10-19}} :This shrine enshrines Kushinadahime as its main deity, with Susanoo and [[Ōyamatsumi]] serving as auxiliary deities.{{cite web |title=県内神社一覧 |url=http://kensaku.shimane-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja_okuizumo.php |website=Shimane-ken Jinjachō |access-date=2020-10-21}} Near the shrine is the Ubuyu-no-Ike (産湯の池, lit. "Birth-Bath Pond"), a pond claimed to be the place where Kushinadahime received her first bath (''ubuyu'') after being born, and a {{ill|Sasa (plant)|en|Sasa (plant)|qid=Q2322484|lt=sasa|1=Sasa (plant)}} bamboo grove that is said to have grown out of the bamboo {{ill|Spatula|en|Spatula|qid=Q15148|lt=Spatula|1=Spatula}} (''hera'') that was used to cut the newborn Kushinadahime's {{ill|Umbilical cord|en|Umbilical cord|qid=Q172563|lt=Umbilical cord|1=Umbilical cord}} known as the Sasa-no-Miya (笹の宮).{{cite web |title=稲田神社 (Inada-jinja) |url=https://okuizumo.org/jp/guide/detail/215/ |website=奥出雲町公式観光ガイド (The Official Okuizumo Travel Guide) |access-date=2020-10-19}}{{cite web |title=笹宮 (Sasa-no-Miya) |url=https://okuizumo.org/jp/guide/detail/176/ |website=奥出雲町公式観光ガイド (The Official Okuizumo Travel Guide) |access-date=2020-10-21}} *[[:ja:八重垣神社|Yaegaki Shrine]], in {{ill|Matsue|en|Matsue|qid=Q207321|lt=Matsue|1=Matsue}}, Shimane Prefecture :Kushinadahime is one of this shrine's deities alongside Susanoo, Ōnamuchi (Ōkuninushi) and Aohata-Sakusahiko (one of Susanoo's children recorded in the Izumo ''Fudoki''). As mentioned above, shrine legend claims that Susanoo hid Kushinadahime in the wooded area within the shrine's precincts known as Sakusame Forest (佐久佐女の森 ''Sakusame no mori'') during his battle with the Yamata no Orochi. * [[:ja:須佐神社 (出雲市)|Susa Shrine]] in {{ill|Izumo|en|Izumo|qid=Q301580|lt=Izumo|1=Izumo}}, Shimane Prefecture :This shrine's deities are Susanoo, Kushinadahime, Tenazuchi and Ashinazuchi.{{cite web |title=Dedicated Kami (deities or Japanese gods) |url=http://english.susa-jinja.jp/information/7 |website=Suga Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-03-30}} Located in the former township of Susa (須佐郷), a place closely associated with Susanoo; indeed, a legend recorded in the Izumo ''Fudoki'' states that Susanoo himself enshrined his spirit here.{{cite book |title=Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries |year=1997 |publisher=Association for Asian Studies, Inc. |translator=Aoki, Michiko Y.|pages=140–141}}{{cite web |title=History |url=http://english.susa-jinja.jp/information/24 |website=Suga Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-03-30}} The shrine's priestly lineage, the Susa (or Inada) clan (須佐氏 / 稲田氏), were considered to be Susanoo's descendants via his son Yashimashino-no-Mikoto (八島篠命, the ''Kojiki'''s Yashimajinumi){{cite book |title=飯石郡誌 (Iishi-gun shi) |year=1918 |publisher=飯石郡役所 (Iishi-gun yakusho) |page=247 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rh3lGVy1zLMC&pg=PP347 |language=ja}}{{cite book |title=大日本神社志 (Dai-Nippon jinja shi) |year=1933 |publisher=大日本敬神会本部 (Dai-Nippon Keishinkai Honbu) |page=342 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X7ut5gI2vQkC&pg=PP626}} or Ōkuninushi.{{cite web |title=須佐(稲田)氏 (Susa (Inada)-shi) |url=http://www.harimaya.com/o_kamon1/syake/south/s_susa.html |website=家紋World - World of KAMON |access-date=2020-03-30}} * [[:ja:須我神社|Suga Shrine]] in [[:en:Unnan, Shimane|Unnan]], Shimane Prefecture :This shrine is claimed to stand on the site of the palace Susanoo built after defeating the Yamata no Orochi and enshrines Susanoo, Kushinadahime, and their son Suga-no-Yuyamanushi-Minasarohiko-Yashima-no-Mikoto (清之湯山主三名狭漏彦八島野命, i.e. Yashimajinumi).{{cite web |title=第十六番 須我神社 |url=https://shinbutsu.jp/shrines-temples/sugajinja/ |website=出雲國神仏霊場を巡る旅 (Izumo-no-kuni shinbutsu reijo o meguru tabi) |publisher=社寺縁座の会 (Shaji Enza no Kai) |access-date=2020-03-30}} * [[:ja:櫛田宮|Kushida Shrine]] (櫛田宮 ''Kushida-gū'') in {{ill|Kanzaki, Saga|en|Kanzaki, Saga|qid=Q990392|lt=Kanzaki|1=Kanzaki, Saga}}, {{ill|Saga Prefecture|en|Saga Prefecture|qid=Q160420|lt=Saga Prefecture|1=Saga Prefecture}} :Dedicated to Susanoo, Kushinadahime, and {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}. Legend claims that the shrine was founded by Yamato Takeru's father {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, who visited the area and enshrined these three deities. A [[:en:Camphor tree|Camphor tree]] in the shrine grounds is said to have grown out of a ''{{ill|Koto (instrument)|en|Koto (instrument)|qid=Q289037|lt=koto|1=Koto (instrument)}}'' that the emperor buried in the ground.{{cite web |title=沿革概要 |url=http://www5b.biglobe.ne.jp/~kusidagu/enkaku/enkaku.html |website=Kushida-gū Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} * [[:ja:櫛田神社 (射水市)|Kushida Shrine]] (櫛田神社 ''Kushida-jinja'') in [[:en:Imizu, Toyama|Imizu]], {{ill|Toyama Prefecture|en|Toyama Prefecture|qid=Q132929|lt=Toyama Prefecture|1=Toyama Prefecture}} :This shrine, claimed to have been founded by [[Takenouchi no Sukune]], enshrines Susanoo and Kushinadahime as its principal deities.{{cite web |title=神社・境内案内 |url=http://kushida.main.jp/pg126.html |website=Kushida Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} * [[Yasaka Shrine]] in [[Gion]], {{ill|Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto|en|Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto|qid=Q1203862|lt=Higashiyama|1=Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto}}, {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}{{cite web |title=御祭神 |url=http://www.yasaka-jinja.or.jp/about/saijin.html |website=Yasaka Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} * [[:ja:広峯神社|Hiromine Shrine]] in {{ill|Himeji|en|Himeji|qid=Q209801|lt=Himeji|1=Himeji}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|qid=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}}{{cite web |title=神々のご利益一覧 |url=http://www.hiromine-j.jp/04goriyaku/image/goriyaku.pdf |website=Hiromine Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} *[[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]] in {{ill|Ōmiya-ku, Saitama|en|Ōmiya-ku, Saitama|qid=Q153629|lt=Ōmiya|1=Ōmiya-ku, Saitama}}, [[:en:Saitama, Saitama|Saitama]], {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture|1=Saitama Prefecture}} :The ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|qid=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province|1=Musashi Province}}, dedicated to Susanoo, Kushinadahime, and Ōnamuchi.{{cite web |title=氷川神社について |url=http://musashiichinomiya-hikawa.or.jp/about/index.html |website=Hikawa Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} Many of its [[Shinto shrine#Shrine networks|branch shrines]] - concentrated in {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture|1=Saitama Prefecture}} and {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|qid=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}} - such as {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Akasaka)|en|Hikawa Shrine (Akasaka)|qid=Q3135503|lt=Akasaka Hikawa Shrine|1=Hikawa Shrine (Akasaka)}} ({{ill|Akasaka, Tokyo|en|Akasaka, Tokyo|qid=Q416131|lt=Akasaka|1=Akasaka, Tokyo}}, {{ill|Minato, Tokyo|en|Minato, Tokyo|qid=Q190088|lt=Minato City|1=Minato, Tokyo}}, Tokyo) or {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Kawagoe)|en|Hikawa Shrine (Kawagoe)|qid=Q11549607|lt=Kawagoe Hikawa Shrine|1=Hikawa Shrine (Kawagoe)}} ({{ill|Kawagoe, Saitama|en|Kawagoe, Saitama|qid=Q319740|lt=Kawagoe|1=Kawagoe, Saitama}}, Saitama){{cite web |title=About Akasaka Hikawa Shrine |url=https://www.akasakahikawa.or.jp/about/en/ |website=Akasaka Hikawa Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19}} also venerate these three deities, though some either enshrine Susanoo alone or pair him with other gods (e.g. [[:ja:氷川神社 (東京都港区元麻布)|Azabu Hikawa Shrine]] in {{ill|Moto-Azabu|en|Moto-Azabu|qid=Q6917930|lt=Moto-Azabu|1=Moto-Azabu}}, Minato, Tokyo, dedicated to Susanoo and Yamato Takeru{{cite web |title=麻布氷川神社について |url=https://www.azabuhikawa.or.jp/about/ |website=Azabu Hikawa Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-10-21 |language=ja}}). *[[:ja:稲田神社|Inada Shrine]] in {{ill|Kasama, Ibaraki|en|Kasama, Ibaraki|qid=Q845851|lt=Kasama|1=Kasama, Ibaraki}}, {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|qid=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}} :This shrine to Kushinadahime is classified in the ''Jinmyōchō'' ([[:ja:延喜式神名帳|神名帳]], lit. 'Register of Shrine Names') section of the ''[[Engishiki]]'' as a 'notable shrine' or ''{{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|qid=Q5369590|lt=myōjin-taisha|1=Myōjin}}'', attesting to its status since antiquity.{{cite web |title=稲田神社（常陸国新治郡） |url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/206003.html |website=Shinto Jinja Database |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2020-10-22}}{{cite web |title=稲田神社 |url=http://www.ibaraki-jinjacho.jp/ibaraki/kenou/jinja/03116.html |website=Ibaraki-ken Jinjachō |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} The shrine's original site is located some 300 meters northwest of the current location, situated beside a spring-fed pond known as Yoshii (好井). According to legend, Kushinadahime appeared to a child who was drawing water from the spring and asked that shrines dedicated to her, her husband Susanoo, and her parents Tenazuchi and Ashinazuchi be built there.{{cite web |title=奥の院 稲田姫伝説の好井 |url=https://craftcouncil-kasama.jp/posts/postDetail?id=18 |website=Craft Council KASAMA JAPAN |access-date=2020-10-22}}{{cite book |editor=Meiji Jinja Shiryō Hensanjo |title=府県郷社 明治神社誌料 上 (Fu-ken-gōsha Meiji Jinja Shiryō, vol. 1) |date=1912 |publisher=Meiji Jinja Shiryō Hensanjo |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1088244/597}} ===Kushinadahime and Harisaijo=== [[File:Harisainyo.png|thumb|180px|Harisai Tennyo, from the ''[[Butsuzōzui]]'']] During the medieval and early modern periods, Susanoo was popularly conflated with the pestilence deity [[:ja:牛頭天王|Gozu Tennō]], the god originally worshiped in Yasaka Shrine in Kyoto, Hiromine Shrine in Hyōgo Prefecture, and [[:ja:津島神社|Tsushima Shrine]] in Tsushima, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|qid=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}.{{cite web |last1=Yonei |first1=Tsuruyoshi |title=Gozu Tennō |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=192 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2020-10-19}} As Susanoo's consort, Kushinadahime was in turn identified with Gozu Tennō's wife, [[:ja:頗梨采女|Harisaijo]] (頗梨采女 or 波利采女, also known as 'Harisainyo', 'Barisainyo', or 'Harisai {{ill|Tennin|en|Tennin|qid=Q7700291|lt=Tennyo|1=Tennin}}' (頗梨采天女)), the third daughter of the dragon (''[[nāga]]'') king {{ill|Sāgara (Dragon King)|en|Sāgara (Dragon King)|qid=Q85804720|lt=Sāgara|1=Sāgara (Dragon King)}}.{{cite book |last1=Rambelli |first1=Fabio |title=Buddhist Materiality: A Cultural History of Objects in Japanese Buddhism |date=2007 |publisher=Stanford University Press |pages=230–231}}{{cite book |last1=Brumann |first1=Christoph |title=Tradition, Democracy and the Townscape of Kyoto: Claiming a Right to the Past |date=2012 |publisher=Routledge |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=umxl_19elUQC&pg=PA166|page=166|isbn=9780415690706 }} Indeed, while Yasaka Shrine in Kyoto currently enshrines Susanoo, his wives (Kushinadahime, Kamu-Ōichihime, and Samirahime), and his eight children (Yashimajinumi, [[Isotakeru-no-Mikoto|I(so)takeru]], Ōya(tsu)hime, Tsumatsuhime, [[Toshigami|Ōtoshi]], [[Ukanomitama]], [[Oyabiko]], and [[Suseri-Hime|Suseribime]]), its original deities were Gozu Tennō, Harisaijo, and their eight sons, collectively known as the 'Eight Princes' (八王子, ''Hachiōji'').{{cite book |last1=Shimada |first1=Hiromi |title=Ekibyō-taisan. Nihon no gofu besuto 10 (疫病退散 日本の護符ベスト10) |date=2020 |publisher=Cyzo |page=25 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kt_3DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA25}} == Legacy == The asteroid {{ill|10613 Kushinadahime|en|10613 Kushinadahime|qid=Q2636622|lt=10613 Kushinadahime|1=10613 Kushinadahime}}, discovered in 1997, is named after Kushinadahime. Kushinadahime was portrayed by {{ill|Misa Uehara|en|Misa Uehara|qid=Q3316207|lt=Misa Uehara|1=Misa Uehara}} in the 1959 film ''[[:en:The Birth of Japan|The Birth of Japan]]''. In the {{ill|Nintendo|en|Nintendo|qid=Q8093|lt=Nintendo|1=Nintendo}} video game {{ill|Golden Sun: The Lost Age|en|Golden Sun: The Lost Age|qid=Q2342264|lt=Golden Sun: The Lost Age|1=Golden Sun: The Lost Age}}, characters named ''Kushinada'' and ''Susa'' are roughly based on Kushinadahime and Susanoo. ==Family tree== {{Eight generations of Izumo}} ==See also== *[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] *[[Somin Shōrai]] == References == {{reflist|2}} ==External links== *{{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category-inline|Kushinadahime}} {{Japanese mythology}} [[en:Kushinadahime]] {{Commons category|Kushinadahime}} [[de:Kushinadahime]] [[es:Kushinadahime]] [[fr:Kushinada-hime]] [[it:Kushinadahime]] [[ja:クシナダヒメ]] [[mni:ꯀꯨꯁꯤꯅꯗꯍꯤꯃꯦ]] [[ru:Кусинада-химэ]] [[simple:Kushinadahime]] [[sr:Кушинадахиме]] [[zh:櫛名田比賣]] {{wikidata link|Q505469}} [[Category:Agricultural goddesses]] [[Category:Childhood goddesses]] [[Category:Food goddesses]] [[Category:Gion cult]] [[Category:Japanese goddesses]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Shinto kami]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with 50+ untranslated japanese characters]] [[Category:Pages with 100+ untranslated japanese characters]] [[Category:Pages with 150+ untranslated japanese characters]] [[Category:Pages with 200+ untranslated japanese characters]]

{{Infobox person|gender={{ill|female|qid=Q6581072|1=Female (gender)}}|spouse={{ill|Susanoo|qid=Q272993|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}|children={{ill|Yashimajinumi no kami|qid=Q55522907|1=Yashimajinumi}}; {{ill|Ōkuninushi|qid=Q276944|1=Ōkuninushi}}}} {{short description|Shinto rice goddess}} {{For|the asteroid|10613 Kushinadahime}} {{Infobox deity | type = Japanese | name = Kushinadahime | image = Susanō no mikoto LCCN2008660593.jpg | caption = [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] and Kushinadahime, by {{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|qid=Q467337|lt=Yoshitoshi|1=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}} | god_of = Goddess of rice, agriculture, marriage, love, childbirth, and child rearing | script_name = Japanese | script = 櫛名田比売 | other_names = Kushiinadahime (奇稲田姫)
Inadahime (稲田媛)
Makamifuru-Kushiinadahime (真髪触奇稲田媛)
Kushiinada-Mitoyomanurahime-no-Mikoto (久志伊奈太美等与麻奴良比売命) | cult_center = [[:ja:須佐神社 (出雲市)|Susa Shrine]], [[Yaegaki Shrine]], [[:ja:須我神社|Suga Shrine]], [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]], [[Yasaka Shrine]], [[:ja:広峯神社|Hiromine Shrine]], [[:ja:櫛田神社 (射水市)|Kushida Shrine (Saga)]], [[:ja:櫛田宮|Kushida Shrine (Toyama)]] and others | symbols = | consort =[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]]; {{ill|Susanoo|qid=Q272993|1=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}| parents = [[Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi|Ashimazuchi]] and [[Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi|Temazuchi]] | siblings = Unnamed seven sisters | children = [[Yashimajinumi]] (''Kojiki'')
[[Ōkuninushi|Ōnamuchi]] (''Nihon Shoki'') | texts = ''[[Kojiki]]'', ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', ''[[Fudoki|Izumo Fudoki]]'', ''[[:en:Sendai Kuji Hongi|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'' | gender = {{ill|female|qid=Q6581072|1=Female (gender)}} | offspring = {{ill|Yashimajinumi no kami|qid=Q55522907|1=Yashimajinumi}}; {{ill|Ōkuninushi|qid=Q276944|1=Ōkuninushi}} }} {{nihongo|'''Kushinadahime'''|櫛名田比売、くしなだひめ}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kushiinadahime'''|奇稲田姫、くしいなだひめ}} or '''Inadahime''' (稲田姫、いなだひめ) among other names, is a goddess (''[[kami]]'') in [[Japanese mythology]] and the [[Shinto]] faith. According to these traditions, she is one of the wives of the god [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]], who rescued her from the monster {{ill|Yamata no Orochi|en|Yamata no Orochi|qid=Q1054437|lt=Yamata no Orochi|1=Yamata no Orochi}}. As Susanoo's wife, she is a central deity of the [[Gion Faith|Gion cult]] and worshipped at [[Yasaka Shrine]].{{Cite web |date=21 April 2005 |title=Mikogami |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=13 |access-date=29 September 2019 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |archive-date=30 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930212535/http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=13 |url-status=bot: unknown }} ==Name== The goddess is named 'Kushinadahime' (櫛名田比売) in the ''[[Kojiki]]'', while the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' variously names her 'Kushiinadahime' (奇稲田姫), 'Inadahime' (稲田姫), and 'Makamifuru-Kushiinadahime' (真髪触奇稲田媛). 'Inadahime' may be translated either as "lady / princess (''[[:wikt:姫#Etymology 1 2|hime]]'') of Inada", with "Inada" (稲田) here being understood as the name of a place in {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|qid=Q582846|lt=Izumo Province|1=Izumo Province}} (part of what is now the town of [[:en:Okuizumo, Shimane|Okuizumo]] (formerly {{ill|Yokota, Shimane|en|Yokota, Shimane|qid=Q4244768|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota, Shimane}}) in {{ill|Nita District, Shimane|en|Nita District, Shimane|qid=Q1204696|lt=Nita District|1=Nita District, Shimane}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}),{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |year=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |page=473}} or "lady / princess of the rice fields" (''inada'' literally translated means "rice field" or "rice paddy").{{cite book |last1=Aston |first1=William G. |title=Shinto (The Way of the Gods) |date=1905 |publisher=Longmans, Green, and Co. |pages=137–138 |url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/46038/46038-h/46038-h.htm}}{{cite book |last1=Hiraizumi |first1=Kiyoshi |title=The Story of Japan: History from the Founding of the Nation to the Height of Fujiwara Prosperity |date=1997 |publisher=Sekai Shuppan Incorporated |page=25}} The element ''kushi'' ({{ill|Old Japanese|en|Old Japanese|qid=Q5736700|lt=Old Japanese|1=Old Japanese}}: ''kusi'') meanwhile is usually interpreted as the adjective meaning "wondrous"; it is homophonous with the word for "{{ill|Comb|en|Comb|qid=Q23834|lt=Comb|1=Comb}}" (櫛), which features in her story in both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Shoki''.{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |year=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |page=509}} The epithet ''makamifuru'' (lit. "true-hair-touching"), found in a variant account cited in the ''Shoki'', is understood as a stock epithet or ''{{ill|Makurakotoba|en|Makurakotoba|qid=Q845474|lt=Makurakotoba|1=Makurakotoba}}'' associated with the word "comb".{{cite book |last1=Matsuoka |first1=Shizuo |title=Nihon Kogo Daijiten (日本古語大辭典) |date=1929 |publisher=Tōkō Shoin |page=1140 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NMZnXlFd8KsC&pg=PP1174}} The ''[[Fudoki]]'' of Izumo Province meanwhile gives the name of the goddess as 久志伊奈太美等与麻奴良比売命, commonly read as 'Kushiinada-Mitoyomanurahime-no-Mikoto'. One theory interprets the name to mean roughly "princess of the wondrous rice fields (''kushi-inada'') soaking wet (''manura'') [and] overflowing with water (''mitoyo'', here understood as an epithet meaning "water-abundant")".{{cite journal |last1=Yoshino |first1=Yū |title=Kushiinada-Mitoyomanurahime-no-Mikoto ni tsuite (久志伊奈太美等与麻奴良比売命について) |journal=Nihon Bungaku (日本文学) |date=1969 |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=56–61 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/nihonbungaku/18/2/18_KJ00010044668/_pdf/-char/ja |publisher=Japanese Literature Association}} ==Mythology== === The slaying of the Yamata no Orochi === {{see also|Susanoo}} [[File:Susanoo-no-Mikoto-slays-Yamata-no-Orochi-in-Izumo-By-Tsukioka-Yoshitoshi.png|thumb|390px|Susanoo and the {{ill|Yamata no Orochi|en|Yamata no Orochi|qid=Q1054437|lt=Yamata no Orochi|1=Yamata no Orochi}}, by {{ill|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|en|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|qid=Q467337|lt=Yoshitoshi|1=Tsukioka Yoshitoshi}}]] In the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', the god [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]], after his banishment from the heavenly realm [[Takamagahara]], came down to earth, to the {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|qid=Q582846|lt=land of Izumo|1=Izumo Province}}, where he encountered an elderly couple named [[Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi]], both children of the mountain god [[Ōyamatsumi]]. They told him of a monstrous creature from the nearby land of {{ill|Koshi Province (Japan)|en|Koshi Province (Japan)|qid=Q1351611|lt=Koshi|1=Koshi Province (Japan)}} known as the {{ill|Yamata no Orochi|en|Yamata no Orochi|qid=Q1054437|lt=Yamata no Orochi|1=Yamata no Orochi}} ("eight-forked serpent") that had devoured seven of their eight daughters. Upon hearing this, Susanoo agreed to kill the serpent on condition that they give him their sole surviving daughter, Kushinadahime, to be his wife.Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj025.htm Section XVIII.—The Eight-Forked Serpent.]{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |year=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |pages=89–90}} The version recounted in the ''Nihon Shoki'''s main narrative is as follows (translation by [[William George Aston]]): {{blockquote|text=Then Sosa no wo no Mikoto descended from Heaven and proceeded to the head-waters of the River Hi, in the province of Idzumo. At this time he heard a sound of weeping at the head-waters of the river, and he therefore went in search of the sound. He found there an old man and an old woman. Between them was set a young girl, whom they were caressing and lamenting over. Sosa no wo no Mikoto asked them, saying:—"Who are ye, and why do ye lament thus?" The answer was:—"I am an Earthly Deity, and my name is Ashi-nadzuchi. My wife's name is Te-nadzuchi. This girl is our daughter, and her name is Kushi-nada-hime. The reason of our weeping is that formerly we had eight children, daughters. But they have been devoured year after year by an eight-forked serpent, and now the time approaches for this girl to be devoured. There is no means of escape for her, and therefore do we grieve." Sosa no wo no Mikoto said:—"If that is so, wilt thou give me thy daughter?" He replied, and said:—"I will comply with thy behest and give her to thee." Therefore Sosa no wo no Mikoto on the spot changed Kushi-nada-hime into a many-toothed close-comb, which he stuck in the august knot of his hair. Then he made Ashi-nadzuchi and Te-nadzuchi to brew eight-fold [[sake]], to make eight cupboards, in each of them to set a tub filled with sake, and so to await its coming. When the time came, the serpent actually appeared. It had an eight-forked head and an eight-forked tail; its eyes were red, like the winter-cherry; and on its back firs and cypresses were growing. As it crawled it extended over a space of eight hills and eight valleys. Now when it came and found the sake, each head dRank up one tub, and it became drunken and fell asleep. Then Sosa no wo no Mikoto drew the [[Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|ten-span sword]] which he wore, and chopped the serpent into small pieces. When he came to the tail, the edge of his sword was slightly notched, and he therefore split open the tail and examined it. In the inside there was a sword. This is the sword which is called [[Kusanagi no Tsurugi|Kusa-nagi no tsurugi]].{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspages=52-53}}}} After defeating the serpent, Susanoo built a palace or shrine for Kushinadahime in a place called Suga - so named because Susanoo felt refreshed (''sugasugashi'') upon arriving there - and made her father Ashinazuchi its head (''obito''), giving him the title 'Inada-no-Miyanushi-Suga-no-Yatsumimi-no-Kami' (稲田宮主須賀之八耳神 "Master of the Palace of Inada, the Eight-Eared Deity of Suga"). On that occasion, he composed a song in ''{{ill|Tanka|en|Tanka|qid=Q258331|lt=Tanka|1=Tanka}}'' form later held to be the root of Japanese ''{{ill|Waka (poetry)|en|Waka (poetry)|qid=Q737148|lt=waka|1=Waka (poetry)}}'' poetry:{{EOS|Kushinadahime|102|Mori, Mizue|1 January 2014}} :{| ! {{ill|Man'yōgana|en|Man'yōgana|qid=Q862803|lt=Man'yōgana|1=Man'yōgana}} (''Kojiki'')|| || Japanese|| || {{ill|Old Japanese|en|Old Japanese|qid=Q5736700|lt=Old Japanese|1=Old Japanese}} || || Modern Japanese ([[:en:Rōmaji|Rōmaji]]) || || Translated by {{ill|Edwin Cranston|en|Edwin Cranston|qid=Q5346323|lt=Edwin Cranston|1=Edwin Cranston}}{{cite book |translator=Cranston, Edwin A. |title=A Waka Anthology. Volume One: The Gem-Glistening Cup |date=1998 |publisher=Stanford University Press |page=7 |isbn=9780804731577 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KqWjwalbmx4C&pg=PA7}} |- | 夜久毛多都
伊豆毛夜幣賀岐

曾能夜幣賀岐袁{{cite book |last1=Takeda |first1=Yūkichi |title=記紀歌謡集 (Kiki Kayōshu) |date=1948 |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |page=7 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1069683/5}} |   | {{lang|ja|八雲立つ

妻籠みに
八重垣作る
その八重垣を}} |   | ''Yakumo[[Old Japanese#Syllables|1]] tatu

''Based on {{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |year=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press|page=426}} The transcription system used to distinguish type A/B vowels in the original text had been changed to [[Old Japanese#Transcription|indexed notation]]. |   | ''Yakumo tatsu

And, oh, that eightfold fence! |} The child born to Susanoo and Kushinadahime is variously identified as [[Yashimajinumi]] in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and Ōnamuchi ([[Ōkuninushi]]) in the ''Shoki'''s main account.Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj027.htm Section XX.—The August Ancestors of the Deity-Master-of-the-Great-Land.]{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |year=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |page=92}}{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=54}} ====Variants==== [[File:Mt.Sentsuzan.jpg|thumb|290px|{{ill|Mount Sentsū|en|Mount Sentsū|qid=Q6923566|lt=Mount Sentsū|1=Mount Sentsū}} as seen from [[:en:Okuizumo, Shimane|Okuizumo]] with the Hii River in the foreground]] While most accounts identify the headwaters of the river Hi in Izumo (肥河 / 簸之川, ''Hi-no-Kawa'', identified with the {{ill|Hii River|en|Hii River|qid=Q11500714|lt=Hii River|1=Hii River}} in modern {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}) as the place where Susanoo descended, one variant in the ''Shoki'' instead has Susanoo arriving at the upper reaches of the river E (可愛之川 ''E-no-Kawa'') in the province of {{ill|Aki Province|en|Aki Province|qid=Q965029|lt=Aki|1=Aki Province}} (identified with the {{ill|Gōnokawa River|en|Gōnokawa River|qid=Q2090210|lt=Gōnokawa River|1=Gōnokawa River}} in modern {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|qid=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}}). In this version, Inadahime - whose name is given here as 'Makamifuru-Kushiinadahime' (真髪触奇稲田媛) - is not yet born when Susanoo slew the Yamata no Orochi.{{cite wikisource |author-first= William George |author-last= Aston |chapter= Book I |wslink= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |plaintitle= Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |year= 1896 |publisher= Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|wspage=55}}{{cite book |last1=Kuroita |first1=Katsumi |title=Kundoku Nihon Shoki, vol. 1 (訓読日本書紀 上巻) |date=1943 |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |pages=69–71 |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1904260/37}} {{blockquote|text=In one writing it is said:—"At this time Sosa no wo no Mikoto went down and came to the head-waters of the River Ye, in the province of Aki. There was there a God whose name was Ashi-nadzu-te-nadzu. His wife's name was Inada no Miya-nushi Susa no yatsu-mimi. This Deity was just then pregnant, and the husband and wife sorrowed together. So they informed Sosa no wo no Mikoto, saying:—'Though we have had born to us many children, whenever one is born, an eight-forked serpent comes and devours it, and we have not been able to save one. We are now about to have another, and we fear that it also will be devoured. Therefore do we grieve.' Sosa no wo no Mikoto forthwith instructed them, saying:—'You must take fruit of all kinds, and brew from it eight jars of sake, and I will kill the serpent for you.' The two Gods, in accordance with his instructions, prepared sake. When the time came for the child to be born, the serpent came indeed to the door, and was about to devour the child. But Sosa no wo no Mikoto addressed the serpent, and said:—'Thou art an Awful Deity. Can I dare to neglect to feast thee?' So he took the eight jars of sake, and poured one into each of its mouths. The serpent dRank it up and fell asleep. Sosa no wo no Mikoto drew his sword and slew it. [...]
Afterwards the child who was born of Inada no Miya-nushi Susa no yatsu-mimi, namely Ina-gami (''{{ill|Sic|en|Sic|qid=Q192003|lt=Sic|1=Sic}}'') Furu-kushi-nada-hime, was removed to the upper waters of the river Hi, in the province of ldzumo, and brought up there. After this Sosa no wo no Mikoto made her his consort, and had by her a child, whose descendant in the sixth generation was [[Ōkuninushi|Oho-na-muchi no Mikoto]]."|author=translation by William George Aston}} A legend associated with [[:ja:八重垣神社|Yaegaki Shrine]] in {{ill|Matsue|en|Matsue|qid=Q207321|lt=Matsue|1=Matsue}}, Shimane Prefecture claims that Susanoo hid Kushinadahime in an "eightfold fence" (''yaegaki'') in the forest within the shrine's precincts during his battle with the Yamata no Orochi.{{cite web |title=八重垣神社について |url=https://yaegakijinja.or.jp/origin |website=【公式】八重垣神社 (Yaegaki Shrine Official Website) |access-date=2020-03-30}} ===In the Izumo ''Fudoki''=== [[File:Yaegaki Jinja hekiga.jpg|thumb|160px|left|{{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}} wall painting depicting Kushinadahime ([[Yaegaki Shrine]], {{ill|Matsue|en|Matsue|qid=Q207321|lt=Matsue|1=Matsue}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}})]] A legend recorded in the Izumo ''[[Fudoki]]'' concerning the township of Kumatani (熊谷郷) in {{ill|Iishi District, Shimane|en|Iishi District, Shimane|qid=Q1349339|lt=Iishi District|1=Iishi District, Shimane}} (part of the modern city of [[:en:Unnan, Shimane|Unnan]] in Shimane{{cite web |title=飯石郡の村々 |url=https://www.pref.shimane.lg.jp/life/bunka/bunkazai/izumo_fuudo/mura/iish2.html |website=Shimane Prefectural Government Official Website |access-date=2020-10-19}}) relates that Kushinadahime - as 'Kushiinada-Mitoyomanurahime' - passed through the area while she was about to give birth. The township's name is said to come from her exclamation: "How deep and well hidden (''kumakumashiki'') this valley (''tani'') is!"{{cite book |last1=Kurita |first1=Hiroshi |title=標註古風土記 出雲 (Hyōchū Kofudoki: Izumo) |date=1931 |publisher=Ō-Oyakama Shoten. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dSqbfMx0ErgC}}{{cite book |title=Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries. |date=1997 |publisher=Association for Asian Studies, Inc. |translator=Aoki, Michiko Y.|page=40}} ===In the Hōki ''Fudoki''=== An excerpt claimed to be from the now-lost ''Fudoki'' of {{ill|Hōki Province|en|Hōki Province|qid=Q1053703|lt=Hōki Province|1=Hōki Province}} (modern western {{ill|Tottori Prefecture|en|Tottori Prefecture|qid=Q133935|lt=Tottori Prefecture|1=Tottori Prefecture}}) relates that Inadahime fled to Hōki and hid in the mountains when the Yamata no Orochi was about to devour her. The province's name (originally ''Hahaki'') is here said to be derived from her cry for help: "Mother, come!" (''haha kimase''){{cite book |last1=Yano |first1=Harumichi |title=神典翼 第3巻 (Shinten'yoku, vol. 3) |date=1939 |publisher=Kokumin Seishin Bunka Kenkyūjo |page=130|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tFX2M_MiEeYC&pg=PP142}}{{cite web |title=山陰道の旧国－１（伯耆国・Inaba Province ） |url=http://houki.yonago-kodaisi.com/F-geo-Kyuukoku-B1.html |website=米子（西伯耆）・山陰の古代史 (Yonago (Nishi-Hōki) / San'in no Kodaishi) |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}}{{cite web |title=伯耆 (Hōki) |url=http://www.nihonjiten.com/data/247618.html |website=Nihon Jiten (日本辞典) - Japan Dictionary |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} == Worship == [[File:Front shrine of the Hikawa shrine.jpg|thumb|[[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Hikawa Shrine]] in [[:en:Saitama, Saitama|Saitama]], {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture|1=Saitama Prefecture}}]] As with other Shinto ''kami'', Kushinadahime is venerated at many shrines across Japan, usually together with her husband Susanoo but also sometimes by herself or with other (related or unrelated) deities. Some examples of Shinto shrines which enshrine her are as follows. * [[:ja:稲田神社 (奥出雲町)|Inada Shrine]] in [[:en:Okuizumo, Shimane|Okuizumo]], {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}{{cite web |title=稲田神社 |url=https://okuizumo.org/jp/guide/detail/215/ |website=奥出雲町公式観光ガイド (The Official Okuizumo Travel Guide) |access-date=2020-10-19}} :This shrine enshrines Kushinadahime as its main deity, with Susanoo and [[Ōyamatsumi]] serving as auxiliary deities.{{cite web |title=県内神社一覧 |url=http://kensaku.shimane-jinjacho.or.jp/jinja_okuizumo.php |website=Shimane-ken Jinjachō |access-date=2020-10-21}} Near the shrine is the Ubuyu-no-Ike (産湯の池, lit. "Birth-Bath Pond"), a pond claimed to be the place where Kushinadahime received her first bath (''ubuyu'') after being born, and a {{ill|Sasa (plant)|en|Sasa (plant)|qid=Q2322484|lt=sasa|1=Sasa (plant)}} bamboo grove that is said to have grown out of the bamboo {{ill|Spatula|en|Spatula|qid=Q15148|lt=Spatula|1=Spatula}} (''hera'') that was used to cut the newborn Kushinadahime's {{ill|Umbilical cord|en|Umbilical cord|qid=Q172563|lt=Umbilical cord|1=Umbilical cord}} known as the Sasa-no-Miya (笹の宮).{{cite web |title=稲田神社 (Inada-jinja) |url=https://okuizumo.org/jp/guide/detail/215/ |website=奥出雲町公式観光ガイド (The Official Okuizumo Travel Guide) |access-date=2020-10-19}}{{cite web |title=笹宮 (Sasa-no-Miya) |url=https://okuizumo.org/jp/guide/detail/176/ |website=奥出雲町公式観光ガイド (The Official Okuizumo Travel Guide) |access-date=2020-10-21}} *[[:ja:八重垣神社|Yaegaki Shrine]], in {{ill|Matsue|en|Matsue|qid=Q207321|lt=Matsue|1=Matsue}}, Shimane Prefecture :Kushinadahime is one of this shrine's deities alongside Susanoo, Ōnamuchi (Ōkuninushi) and Aohata-Sakusahiko (one of Susanoo's children recorded in the Izumo ''Fudoki''). As mentioned above, shrine legend claims that Susanoo hid Kushinadahime in the wooded area within the shrine's precincts known as Sakusame Forest (佐久佐女の森 ''Sakusame no mori'') during his battle with the Yamata no Orochi. * [[:ja:須佐神社 (出雲市)|Susa Shrine]] in {{ill|Izumo|en|Izumo|qid=Q301580|lt=Izumo|1=Izumo}}, Shimane Prefecture :This shrine's deities are Susanoo, Kushinadahime, Tenazuchi and Ashinazuchi.{{cite web |title=Dedicated Kami (deities or Japanese gods) |url=http://english.susa-jinja.jp/information/7 |website=Suga Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-03-30}} Located in the former township of Susa (須佐郷), a place closely associated with Susanoo; indeed, a legend recorded in the Izumo ''Fudoki'' states that Susanoo himself enshrined his spirit here.{{cite book |title=Records of Wind and Earth: A Translation of Fudoki, with Introduction and Commentaries |year=1997 |publisher=Association for Asian Studies, Inc. |translator=Aoki, Michiko Y.|pages=140–141}}{{cite web |title=History |url=http://english.susa-jinja.jp/information/24 |website=Suga Shrine Official Website |access-date=2020-03-30}} The shrine's priestly lineage, the Susa (or Inada) clan (須佐氏 / 稲田氏), were considered to be Susanoo's descendants via his son Yashimashino-no-Mikoto (八島篠命, the ''Kojiki'''s Yashimajinumi){{cite book |title=飯石郡誌 (Iishi-gun shi) |year=1918 |publisher=飯石郡役所 (Iishi-gun yakusho) |page=247 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rh3lGVy1zLMC&pg=PP347 |language=ja}}{{cite book |title=大日本神社志 (Dai-Nippon jinja shi) |year=1933 |publisher=大日本敬神会本部 (Dai-Nippon Keishinkai Honbu) |page=342 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X7ut5gI2vQkC&pg=PP626}} or Ōkuninushi.{{cite web |title=須佐(稲田)氏 (Susa (Inada)-shi) |url=http://www.harimaya.com/o_kamon1/syake/south/s_susa.html |website=家紋World - World of KAMON |access-date=2020-03-30}} * [[:ja:須我神社|Suga Shrine]] in [[:en:Unnan, Shimane|Unnan]], Shimane Prefecture :This shrine is claimed to stand on the site of the palace Susanoo built after defeating the Yamata no Orochi and enshrines Susanoo, Kushinadahime, and their son Suga-no-Yuyamanushi-Minasarohiko-Yashima-no-Mikoto (清之湯山主三名狭漏彦八島野命, i.e. Yashimajinumi).{{cite web |title=第十六番 須我神社 |url=https://shinbutsu.jp/shrines-temples/sugajinja/ |website=出雲國神仏霊場を巡る旅 (Izumo-no-kuni shinbutsu reijo o meguru tabi) |publisher=社寺縁座の会 (Shaji Enza no Kai) |access-date=2020-03-30}} * [[:ja:櫛田宮|Kushida Shrine]] (櫛田宮 ''Kushida-gū'') in {{ill|Kanzaki, Saga|en|Kanzaki, Saga|qid=Q990392|lt=Kanzaki|1=Kanzaki, Saga}}, {{ill|Saga Prefecture|en|Saga Prefecture|qid=Q160420|lt=Saga Prefecture|1=Saga Prefecture}} :Dedicated to Susanoo, Kushinadahime, and {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}. Legend claims that the shrine was founded by Yamato Takeru's father {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, who visited the area and enshrined these three deities. 'Register of Shrine Names') section of the ''[[Engishiki]]'' as a 'notable shrine' or ''{{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|qid=Q5369590|lt=myōjin-taisha|1=Myōjin}}'', attesting to its status since antiquity.{{cite web |title=稲田神社（常陸国新治郡） |url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/206003.html |website=Shinto Jinja Database |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2020-10-22}}{{cite web |title=稲田神社 |url=http://www.ibaraki-jinjacho.jp/ibaraki/kenou/jinja/03116.html |website=Ibaraki-ken Jinjachō |access-date=2020-10-19 |language=ja}} The shrine's original site is located some 300 meters northwest of the current location, situated beside a spring-fed pond known as Yoshii (好井). According to legend, Kushinadahime appeared to a child who was drawing water from the spring and asked that shrines dedicated to her, her husband Susanoo, and her parents Tenazuchi and Ashinazuchi be built there.{{cite web |title=奥の院 稲田姫伝説の好井 |url=https://craftcouncil-kasama.jp/posts/postDetail?id=18 |website=Craft Council KASAMA JAPAN |access-date=2020-10-22}}{{cite book |editor=Meiji Jinja Shiryō Hensanjo |title=府県郷社 明治神社誌料 上 (Fu-ken-gōsha Meiji Jinja Shiryō, vol. 1) |date=1912 |publisher=Meiji Jinja Shiryō Hensanjo |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1088244/597}} ===Kushinadahime and Harisaijo=== [[File:Harisainyo.png|thumb|180px|Harisai Tennyo, from the ''[[Butsuzōzui]]'']] During the medieval and early modern periods, Susanoo was popularly conflated with the pestilence deity [[:ja:牛頭天王|Gozu Tennō]], the god originally worshiped in Yasaka Shrine in Kyoto, Hiromine Shrine in Hyōgo Prefecture, and [[:ja:津島神社|Tsushima Shrine]] in Tsushima, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|qid=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}.{{cite web |last1=Yonei |first1=Tsuruyoshi |title=Gozu Tennō |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=192 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2020-10-19}} As Susanoo's consort, Kushinadahime was in turn identified with Gozu Tennō's wife, [[:ja:頗梨采女|Harisaijo]] (頗梨采女 or 波利采女, also known as 'Harisainyo', 'Barisainyo', or 'Harisai {{ill|Tennin|en|Tennin|qid=Q7700291|lt=Tennyo|1=Tennin}}' (頗梨采天女)), the third daughter of the dragon (''[[nāga]]'') king {{ill|Sāgara (Dragon King)|en|Sāgara (Dragon King)|qid=Q85804720|lt=Sāgara|1=Sāgara (Dragon King)}}.{{cite book |last1=Rambelli |first1=Fabio |title=Buddhist Materiality: A Cultural History of Objects in Japanese Buddhism |date=2007 |publisher=Stanford University Press |pages=230–231}}{{cite book |last1=Brumann |first1=Christoph |title=Tradition, Democracy and the Townscape of Kyoto: Claiming a Right to the Past |date=2012 |publisher=Routledge |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=umxl_19elUQC&pg=PA166|page=166|isbn=9780415690706 }} Indeed, while Yasaka Shrine in Kyoto currently enshrines Susanoo, his wives (Kushinadahime, Kamu-Ōichihime, and Samirahime), and his eight children (Yashimajinumi, [[Isotakeru-no-Mikoto|I(so)takeru]], Ōya(tsu)hime, Tsumatsuhime, [[Toshigami|Ōtoshi]], [[Ukanomitama]], [[Oyabiko]], and [[Suseri-Hime|Suseribime]]), its original deities were Gozu Tennō, Harisaijo, and their eight sons, collectively known as the 'Eight Princes' (八王子, ''Hachiōji'').{{cite book |last1=Shimada |first1=Hiromi |title=Ekibyō-taisan. Nihon no gofu besuto 10 (疫病退散 日本の護符ベスト10) |date=2020 |publisher=Cyzo |page=25 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kt_3DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA25}} == Legacy == The asteroid {{ill|10613 Kushinadahime|en|10613 Kushinadahime|qid=Q2636622|lt=10613 Kushinadahime|1=10613 Kushinadahime}}, discovered in 1997, is named after Kushinadahime. Kushinadahime was portrayed by {{ill|Misa Uehara|en|Misa Uehara|qid=Q3316207|lt=Misa Uehara|1=Misa Uehara}} in the 1959 film ''[[:en:The Birth of Japan|The Birth of Japan]]''. In the {{ill|Nintendo|en|Nintendo|qid=Q8093|lt=Nintendo|1=Nintendo}} video game {{ill|Golden Sun: The Lost Age|en|Golden Sun: The Lost Age|qid=Q2342264|lt=Golden Sun: The Lost Age|1=Golden Sun: The Lost Age}}, characters named ''Kushinada'' and ''Susa'' are roughly based on Kushinadahime and Susanoo. ==Family tree== {{Eight generations of Izumo}} ==See also== *[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] *[[Somin Shōrai]] == References == {{reflist|2}} ==External links== *{{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category-inline|Kushinadahime}} {{Japanese mythology}} {{Commons category|Kushinadahime}} {{wikidata link|Q505469|co|commons:Category:Kushinadahime|de|Kushinadahime|en|Kushinadahime|es|Kushinadahime|fr|Kushinada-hime|it|Kushinadahime|ja|クシナダヒメ|mni|ꯀꯨꯁꯤꯅꯗꯍꯤꯃꯦ|ru|Кусинада-химэ|simple|Kushinadahime|sr|Кушинадахиме|zh|櫛名田比賣}} [[Category:Agricultural goddesses]] [[Category:Childhood goddesses]] [[Category:Food goddesses]] [[Category:Gion cult]] [[Category:Japanese goddesses]] [[Category:Kunitsukami]] [[Category:Shinto kami]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with 50+ untranslated japanese characters]] [[Category:Pages with 100+ untranslated japanese characters]] [[Category:Pages with 150+ untranslated japanese characters]] [[Category:Pages with 200+ untranslated japanese characters]]
